fichas.texto: Semaglutide 0.25→2.4mg/wk. Tirzepatide 2.5→10-15mg/wk. Indication: BMI≥30, or ≥27+comorbidity. ⚠️ "Ozempic babies" (restores ovulation), reduces OCP efficacy, stop ≥2 months preconception, risk of sarcopenia. Non-response rates (<5% weight loss) by pivotal trial: STEP-1 (semaglutide 2.4mg, non-diabetic adults) 13.6% · STEP-TEENS (semaglutide 2.4mg, adolescents with excess-weight comorbidity) 27% · SURMOUNT-1 (tirzepatide 15mg, non-diabetic adults) 9% · STEP-2 (semaglutide 2.4mg, diabetic adults) 31.2% — response is consistently lower in patients with concomitant type 2 diabetes, a point to anticipate when counseling on expectations. Maintaining weight loss requires continuing the medication (STEP 4 with semaglutide and SURMOUNT-4 with tirzepatide): in both trials, patients who, on reaching a weight-loss plateau, were randomized to continue the drug maintained or further deepened their weight loss, while those switched to placebo progressively regained weight over the remaining follow-up — obesity behaves here as a chronic condition requiring sustained treatment, not as a short course with a permanent outcome. GLP-1/GIP + hormone therapy in the climacteric (retrospective cohort, Mayo Clinic): Castaneda et al. (The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health. 2026;2(2):e118-e128), in 120 postmenopausal women with overweight/obesity on tirzepatide (40 on HRT vs. 80 without, propensity-matched), reported that at 15 months HRT users had 35% greater total body weight loss than non-users, along with additional cardiometabolic improvements in both groups. ⚠️ This is retrospective matched-cohort evidence, not a randomized trial — it suggests a possible synergy but does not establish causality, nor does it by itself change the indication for HRT, which should be decided on its own criteria (see the MRS Scale and HRT guide). Note: the preliminary figure presented at the ENDO 2025 congress (~17% vs. 14%) differs from the final Lancet publication — this guide uses the final published figure (35% relative difference), not the preliminary congress figure.
fichas.fuentes: AACE/ACE · Endocrine Society · SURMOUNT/STEP · Austin GO, et al. Front Mol Biosci 2023;10:1170181 · Davies M, et al. Lancet 2021;397(10278):971-984 · Rubino D, et al. JAMA 2021;325(14):1414-1425 (STEP 4) · Aronne LJ, et al. JAMA 2024;331(1):38-48 (SURMOUNT-4) · Castaneda R, et al. The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health. 2026;2(2):e118-e128. doi:10.1016/S3050-5038(25)00145-1

fichas.titulo: EASO 2026 — Algorithm for the pharmacological treatment of obesity and its complications
fichas.texto: An EASO decision framework that separates two treatment goals depending on whether obesity-associated complications are present — not a single "weight loss" algorithm, but one that guides drug choice by the outcome being targeted: No complications (mechanical adiposity) — goal: total body weight loss (TBWL): available options (evidence published through Nov 21, 2025, ranked from highest to lowest relative efficacy vs. placebo): tirzepatide, semaglutide, phentermine-topiramate, liraglutide, naltrexone-bupropion, orlistat. Complications present (metabolic adiposity — deranged endocrine-immune responses) — goal: reverse the affected organ's dysfunction, not just lower weight: OSAS (remission): tirzepatide. Knee osteoarthritis/KOA (pain remission): semaglutide, liraglutide. Prediabetes (normoglycemia restoration): semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide. Type 2 diabetes (remission): tirzepatide, semaglutide, liraglutide, naltrexone-bupropion. Cardiovascular disease (MACE reduction): semaglutide, naltrexone-bupropion. Heart failure (reduced hospitalization): tirzepatide, semaglutide. MASLD/MASH (MASH remission): tirzepatide, semaglutide — new in 2026: liver fibrosis improvement with semaglutide. The original framework also lists, for each endpoint, the drugs in the same class without available evidence for that specific indication (e.g., orlistat has no MASH remission data) — a drug's absence for a given endpoint does not imply demonstrated inefficacy, only a lack of published evidence as of the framework's cutoff date. Consult the original source for the full drug-by-endpoint detail.
fichas.fuentes: Valentinuzzi G, Müller-Wieland D, Holm JC, et al. Framework for the pharmacological treatment of obesity and its complications from the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO): 2026 update. Nat Med. 2026

fichas.texto: Quick-reference map of incretin agonists beyond the 3 already approved (semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide — see GLP-1/GIP analogs guide). None of the following yet has approval for general clinical use; they are listed for context and to anticipate patient questions, not as a use recommendation. Closest to approval (per the source's timeline, subject to change): Oral semaglutide: GLP-1, oral daily, Novo Nordisk. CagriSema (semaglutide + cagrilintide): GLP-1 + amylin receptor co-agonist, SC weekly, Novo Nordisk. Encoglutide (XW003): GLP-1, SC weekly, Sciwind (in development in China). Orforglipron (LY3502970): GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist, oral daily, Eli Lilly. Mazdutide: GLP-1/glucagon receptor co-agonist, SC weekly, Eli Lilly/Innovent (in development in China). Survodutide (BI 456906): GLP-1/glucagon receptor co-agonist, SC weekly, Boehringer Ingelheim. Retatrutide (LY343794): GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist, SC, Eli Lilly — this is the molecule mentioned in the Preconception washout guide as "under investigation." Pemvidutide: GLP-1/glucagon receptor co-agonist, SC weekly, Altimmune. Earlier-stage development / distinct mechanisms: Cagrilintide (AM833): GLP-1/amylin co-agonist, SC weekly, Novo Nordisk. Amycretin: amylin receptor and GLP-1 co-agonist, SC and oral under investigation, Novo Nordisk. Maridebart cafraglutide (AMG-133): GLP-1/GIP co-agonist, SC weekly, Amgen. Bimagrumab: monoclonal antibody blocking activin signaling (not an incretin agonist), IV infusion every 4 weeks, Versanis/Eli Lilly. Danuglipron: GLP-1 agonist, oral, Pfizer — discontinued development: after completing Phase 2, Phase 3 planning was cancelled due to hepatic adverse effects; kept in this list only as historical reference, not as an active candidate. APH-012 / SYNTH-101: oral capsule that simulates the effect of gastric bypass (duodenal lining, stimulates the small intestine), Phase 2 in development, APHAIA FARMA/SYNTIS BIO. ARD-101: oral agonist targeting taste receptors (denatonium), activates endogenous GLP-1/GLP-2/cholecystokinin, finishing Phase 2, Aardvark Therapeutics. CT-388: GLP-1/GIP co-agonist, SC weekly, Structure Therapeutics. VK2735: GLP-1/GIP co-agonist, SC weekly, Viking Pharmaceuticals. HU6: "controlled metabolic accelerator" (distinct mechanism, not an incretin), oral daily, Rivus Pharmaceuticals. INV-202: CB1 blocker, oral daily, Novo Nordisk. EC5004: GLP-1 agonist, oral daily, AstraZeneca/Eccogene. GSBR-1290: GLP-1 agonist, oral daily, Structure Therapeutics. ⚠️ None of these investigational molecules has, as of this guide, reproductive safety studies or a validated preconception washout recommendation — for any patient in a clinical trial with one of these, strictly follow the study's own contraception protocol; do not extrapolate the semaglutide/tirzepatide windows. Timeline and availability taken from the original source (clinicaltrials.gov and company websites, at the time of the presentation) — these can change; verify current regulatory status before discussing with a patient.
fichas.fuentes: AMMR (Asociación Mexicana de Medicina de la Reproducción). "The Incretin Pipeline" — Fig. 2: Current GLP-1 agonist anti-obesity medications and expected upcoming anti-obesity medications. Information from clinicaltrials.gov and/or company websites; presentation by Dr. Eduardo W. Goicochea

fichas.texto: Insulin resistance is a central pathophysiological axis in most patients with PMOS — including many without obesity, according to the Teede et al. 2026 consensus itself that renamed PCOS to PMOS —, not merely an associated comorbidity. Within this, the prevalence of insulin resistance is higher in phenotypes A and B (see the PCOS/PMOS phenotypes guide) than in C/D, per the general PCOS/PMOS phenotype literature (a consistent finding across several case-control studies and meta-analyses, not specific to the Teede paper). This underlies the growing interest in GLP-1/GIP agonists as a metabolic approach in PMOS with an obesity/insulin-resistance component, and in classic insulin sensitizers (metformin, myo-inositol — see next guide) as non-hormonal first-line treatment for ovulatory dysfunction. Recent supporting evidence: Carmina & Longo (J Clin Med, July 2026) treated 96 women with PMOS and overweight/obesity with semaglutide for 6 months — 52.5% of those previously anovulatory achieved ovulatory cycles, with a response strongly dependent on the degree of obesity (~95% menstrual normalization in overweight vs. ~25% in moderate-severe obesity). The authors propose considering GLP-1 before other fertility interventions in obese patients with PMOS — this is prospective cohort evidence, not a trial that has changed society guidelines. ⚠️ Off-label / evolving use: GLP-1/GIP agonists improve ovulation indirectly (weight loss + improved insulin sensitivity), not through a direct reproductive mechanism. Their formal indication remains the management of obesity/type 2 diabetes — despite the cohort evidence cited above, use specifically directed at PMOS does not yet have endorsement from reproductive society guidelines (ASRM, ESHRE, FLASOG) as a primary indication; approach it as a reasoned extension of its approved metabolic indication, case by case.

fichas.titulo: Myo-inositol — PMOS, ovulation induction, and inadvertent exposure
fichas.texto: Mechanism: myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol are second messengers in the insulin signaling pathway — supplementation improves ovarian insulin sensitivity, reduces compensatory hyperinsulinemia, and thereby favors resumption of ovulatory cycles in PMOS. It is not a drug in the strict sense but a dietary nutrient/supplement, which shapes its reproductive safety profile (see the inadvertent exposure note below). Indication: ovulatory dysfunction in PMOS/metabolic phenotype, as an adjunct or alternative to metformin in patients with digestive intolerance to the latter; also used as an adjuvant in ovulation induction/IVF protocols to improve oocyte quality. Usual dose: Myo-inositol 2-4g/day PO, frequently combined with D-chiro-inositol in the physiological 40:1 ratio (the physiological serum ratio described in healthy ovarian tissue), divided into 1-2 daily doses. Clinical response (resumption of cycles) is expected within 3-6 months of continuous use. Evidence: the Cochrane review (2023 update) on inositol for PMOS-associated subfertility finds low-to-moderate certainty evidence favoring a possible improvement in clinical pregnancy and ovulation rates versus placebo, with meta-analyses by Unfer et al. and Facchinetti et al. also showing benefit on metabolic parameters (HOMA-IR, androgen profile) — overall evidence quality remains limited by study size and heterogeneity. Inadvertent exposure during fertility recovery (relevant in women coming off tirzepatide/semaglutide who are improving their metabolic profile): as a physiological nutrient normally present in the diet rather than a synthetic molecule with dedicated teratogenicity studies, myo-inositol is not subject to the same preconception washout restrictions as GLP-1/GIP analogues — no teratogenic warning signal has been described with continued use during an unrecognized pregnancy, and it has in fact also been studied as a supplement for gestational diabetes prevention in at-risk populations. This does not exempt confirming the pregnancy and reassessing the overall therapeutic plan as soon as it is detected. Specific meta-analysis on myo-inositol and gestational diabetes prevention (Poyatos-León R, et al. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2026;235(5):1024-1036. DOI 10.1016/j.ajog.2026.05.020): 12 randomized controlled trials, 4,765 women without preexisting diabetes (pregnant or planning conception within 6 months), search through April 2025. Myo-inositol supplementation substantially reduced the risk of gestational diabetes versus control (44% relative risk reduction), with no significant differences in hypertensive disorders, cesarean delivery, macrosomia, preterm birth, or neonatal hypoglycemia.

fichas.texto: Phenomenon colloquially described as "Ozempic babies": weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity under GLP-1/GIP treatment can restore spontaneous ovulation in anovulatory women with obesity — sometimes unexpectedly, when the patient assumed she did not need contraception or that the effectiveness of her oral hormonal method was not compromised. ("Ozempic babies" is a descriptive/colloquial term, spread through case reports and medical coverage — it does not correspond to a single formal reference; the underlying clinical basis is the mechanism of ovulatory recovery via weight loss/improved insulin resistance, documented in the international PMOS guideline and in the Carmina & Longo cohort cited in the previous guide.) Direct clinical implication: every patient on GLP-1/GIP treatment who is not seeking pregnancy should receive active counseling on effective contraception, even if she previously had anovulation due to PMOS — recovery of ovulatory cycles can occur before the patient notices the change (recovery of menstrual regularity), which is why it is important to proactively address both contraception and preconception planning from the start of GLP-1/GIP treatment, not only when it is stopped (see the Contraception during tirzepatide and Preconception washout guides).

fichas.texto: Tirzepatide's dual GIP/GLP-1 agonism slows gastric emptying more markedly than pure GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide) — this can reduce the absorption of oral drugs, including oral hormonal contraceptives. Recommendation: use a non-oral contraceptive method, or add a barrier method, for 4 weeks after starting tirzepatide and after each dose escalation — not only once at treatment start. ⚠️ Do not confuse with preconception washout (next guide): this 4-week window is due to a pharmacokinetic interaction with the oral contraceptive, while preconception washout is the recommended time to stop the drug before trying to conceive — two distinct concepts, with different durations, and both may apply to the same patient at different times. Practical approach for a patient on tirzepatide who is losing weight and recovering fertility, and who is not seeking pregnancy: prefer non-oral methods whenever possible — LARC (subdermal implant, IUD/IUS — see LARC guide), injectable (DMPA), patch, or vaginal ring — since these do not depend on gastrointestinal absorption and sidestep the underlying problem; if the patient already uses or prefers an oral contraceptive, add a barrier method (condom) for the 4 weeks after starting and after each dose escalation, without needing to stop the oral agent. Discuss contraception from the start of GLP-1/GIP treatment in every woman of reproductive age, not only when she presents seeking pregnancy (see the GLP-1 and fertility recovery guide). Imbroane et al. (AJOG 2025, observational preconception cohort of 8,534 women) document the underlying clinical context — women recovering ovulatory cycles and fertility during GLP-1/GIP use — that supports the need for this proactive contraceptive conversation, although the study does not directly evaluate contraceptive failure rates.

fichas.texto: Semaglutide: the 2026 FDA Wegovy label recommends stopping ≥2 months before trying to conceive, due to its prolonged half-life (~1 week, ~5 half-lives for near-complete elimination). Tirzepatide: here the regulatory agencies differ, and CaVeSal presents both positions without resolving them, so you can decide according to the patient's context: the European label (EMA/Lilly Mounjaro SmPC) recommends stopping ≥1 month before trying to conceive; the U.S. prescribing information (FDA, Zepbound) does not set a mandatory preconception window and instead instructs discontinuing upon recognizing pregnancy — reflecting a genuine difference in regulatory stance, not an error in either source. Liraglutide (daily dosing, shorter half-life): common practice uses a shorter washout window (on the order of 1 week), although it is less standardized in the guidelines than semaglutide/tirzepatide. Dulaglutide, exenatide, lixisenatide: the labels of these older molecules do not set a specific preconception washout window the way semaglutide/tirzepatide do — the usual instruction is to discontinue upon confirming pregnancy, with no preconception interval validated by dedicated studies. ⚠️ Absence of a validated interval does not mean "no need to stop before trying to conceive" — in the absence of specific data, a prudent approach is to apply a criterion similar to semaglutide (weekly-order half-lives) for weekly-depot dulaglutide and exenatide, and one closer to liraglutide for short-acting exenatide/lixisenatide (daily dosing). Retatrutide: a triple GLP-1/GIP/glucagon agonist still under investigation — not approved for general clinical use as of this guide (see the Incretin development pipeline guide). It therefore has no indication or label for use in a population seeking pregnancy; any exposure would occur in the context of a clinical trial, with its own study-specific contraception/washout protocol — do not extrapolate the windows above to this molecule. Imbroane et al. (AJOG 2025;233(2):116.e1-e7; n=4,267 per cohort after matching, 8,534 total) found, in their retrospective preconception cohort (TriNetX), an association with lower incidence of gestational diabetes (18.2% vs. 15.2%; OR 0.81; 95% CI 0.72-0.91), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (22.8% vs. 19.9%; OR 0.84; 95% CI 0.76-0.94), preterm delivery (4.4% vs. 3.0%; OR 0.68; 95% CI 0.54-0.85), and cesarean delivery (19.7% vs. 17.6%; OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.87-0.97) in the group with prior GLP-1/GIP prescription versus the unexposed group. ⚠️ Before matching, the exposed group had a much higher prevalence of overweight/obesity (76.8% vs. 10.7%), type 2 diabetes (37.6% vs. 1.5%), hypertension (32.5% vs. 3.7%), and prior GDM (25.3% vs. 10.0%) — matching adjusted only for age/race/ethnicity/comorbidity categories, not finely for these factors, so much of this apparent protection may reflect residual confounding by indication (who receives GLP-1/GIP) rather than a true protective drug effect. This does not change this guide's preconception washout recommendation — see also the Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide guide for a contrasting read on maternal metabolic/hypertensive outcomes.

fichas.titulo: Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide — what the evidence shows
fichas.texto: Immediate management of an inadvertent pregnancy in a patient using GLP-1/GIP: Stop the drug as soon as pregnancy is confirmed — current evidence does not support continuing it during gestation, regardless of the duration of periconceptional exposure that has already occurred. Reassess the patient's overall metabolic management plan (glycemia, weight, possible metformin indication — see corresponding guide) now in the context of pregnancy, not of weight loss. There is no indication for pregnancy termination based solely on periconceptional GLP-1/GIP exposure — the conversation with the patient should be grounded in the available evidence (summarized below), which so far shows no consistent signal of harm. What the evidence shows (quick-reference summary, not a substitute for each study's methodological detail): Brown et al. (Ann Intern Med 2026, target trial emulation, n=3,572) found no significant increase in major congenital malformations associated with periconceptional exposure to GLP-1 agonists, using a design that emulates a randomized trial from observational data to reduce confounding by indication. D'Antonio et al. (Med 2026, large-scale meta-analysis, n=2,118,215) likewise found no consistent signal of increased risk of adverse obstetric/neonatal outcomes associated with periconceptional or early-pregnancy exposure to GLP-1/GIP agonists — this being the largest sample-size analysis available to date on the topic. The AJOG 2024 review (PII S0002-9378(24)00864-0) synthesizes the body of evidence available at that time in the same reassuring direction, although — like the rest of this literature — it is based predominantly on observational studies rather than randomized trials specifically designed to assess reproductive safety. ⚠️ All of this evidence is observational (cohorts, target trial emulation, cohort meta-analyses) — absence of a harm signal is not equivalent to definitive evidence of safety, and it does not change the recommendation to stop the drug as soon as pregnancy is recognized, nor the recommendation to respect the preconception washout by molecule when pregnancy is planned (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide). Malformations — additional meta-analysis (Uysal et al., Sci Rep 2026;16:31416): across 7 cohort studies with over 40,000 exposed pregnancies, there was no significant signal for congenital malformations overall (OR 1.11; 95% CI 0.82-1.51) nor for major malformations with first-trimester exposure (OR 1.39; 95% CI 0.73-2.65). An isolated significant signal was found for urinary malformations (OR 1.24; 95% CI 1.05-1.47), based on unadjusted data from only 2 studies — the authors themselves attribute it most likely to residual confounding (underlying maternal diabetes/obesity), not a direct teratogenic effect. No increased signal was found for stillbirth, spontaneous abortion, small for gestational age, or preterm birth. Major congenital malformations — largest sample-size meta-analysis available to date (Liu X, et al. Endocrine Connections 2026;15(7). DOI 10.1530/EC-26-0280): across 6 studies (1 prospective + 5 retrospective) with 286,599 women, of whom 43,577 had periconceptional GLP-1RA exposure, there was no significant difference in the risk of major congenital malformations between exposed and unexposed women (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.96-1.08). No significant signal was found either for preterm birth (RR 1.09; 95% CI 0.80-1.49), large for gestational age (RR 2.31; 95% CI 0.56-9.44), small for gestational age (RR 0.71; 95% CI 0.39-1.27), or stillbirth (RR 1.16; 95% CI 0.24-5.69) — these last three have very wide confidence intervals due to low event numbers, and should be read as "insufficient statistical power to detect a risk if one existed," not as "no risk." The authors themselves note that, given the observational design and limited number of exposed pregnancies, these findings should not be interpreted as proof of safety. Gestational weight gain and complications after stopping the drug (Maya J, et al. JAMA 2025;334(24):2186-2196 — retrospective cohort, Mass General Brigham, n=448 exposed vs. 1,344 unexposed, matched by propensity score 1:3, 84% with obesity): exposure to GLP-1/GIP between 3 years before and 90 days after conception was associated with greater gestational weight gain (mean 13.7kg vs. 10.5kg; difference +3.3kg; 95% CI 2.3-4.2; p<0.001), a higher risk of excess gestational weight gain (65% vs. 49%; RR 1.32; 95% CI 1.19-1.47), of preterm delivery (17% vs. 13%; RR 1.34; 95% CI 1.06-1.69), of gestational diabetes (20% vs. 15%; RR 1.30; 95% CI 1.01-1.68), and of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (46% vs. 36%; RR 1.29; 95% CI 1.12-1.49) — with no difference in birth length, large/small for gestational age, or cesarean delivery. ⚠️ Unlike Liu et al. (above), which looks for a malformation signal, this cohort looks at the pregnant patient's own metabolic/hypertensive outcomes after periconceptional exposure — a different, and to some extent contrasting, perspective to the reassurance conveyed by Imbroane et al. 2025 (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide): "no malformation signal" does not equal "no maternal risk at all." Cohort composed mostly of women with obesity — limits generalization to a non-obese population. Gestational weight gain and hypertensive disorders — independent cohort (Pondugula N, et al. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;147(3):293-302. DOI 10.1097/AOG.0000000000005995): a retrospective cohort distinct from Maya et al. (Yale, n=243 exposed up to 1 year before pregnancy — 103 for pregestational diabetes, 140 for weight management — vs. 175 and 200 unexposed, respectively). Found no association between GLP-1RA exposure and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in either cohort (pregestational diabetes: adjusted OR 0.72; 95% CI 0.42-1.25 · weight management: adjusted OR 0.83; 95% CI 0.45-1.52). There was also no association with gestational weight gain in the pregestational diabetes cohort; in the weight-management cohort, exposure was associated with a lower likelihood of gestational weight gain below recommendations (adjusted OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.18-0.78) — the authors interpret this as a possible rebound weight gain after stopping the drug, not as excess weight gain. ⚠️ Important attribution note: the figures of 65% vs. 49% excess weight gain, 20% vs. 15% gestational diabetes, and 46% vs. 36% hypertensive disorders (above) belong to Maya et al., not to this study — these are two independent cohorts with different findings (Pondugula et al. reports no hypertensive-disorder signal; Maya et al. does).

fichas.titulo: Integrated algorithm — GLP-1/GIP and reproductive planning
fichas.texto: Branch 1 — Patient on GLP-1/GIP treatment who is NOT seeking pregnancy (or has not yet decided): Active contraceptive counseling from the start of treatment, even if she previously had anovulation due to PMOS (see the GLP-1 and fertility recovery guide) — fertility can recover before the patient notices. Prefer non-oral methods (LARC, injectable, patch, ring), especially with tirzepatide; if she uses an oral method, add a barrier method for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose escalation (see the Contraception during tirzepatide guide). Branch 2 — Patient who IS seeking pregnancy (preconception planning): Washout by molecule before attempting to conceive (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide) — different windows for semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide; no validated interval for dulaglutide/exenatide/lixisenatide; retatrutide does not apply, as it is not approved. Reassess baseline metabolic management (metformin, myo-inositol) in a preconception context, not a weight-loss one (see the Metformin in pregnancy and Myo-inositol guides). Preconception folic acid according to risk level (see the Preconception screening and folic acid guide). Branch 3 — Inadvertent pregnancy already confirmed during GLP-1/GIP use: Stop the drug immediately. Reassess the metabolic plan in a pregnancy context, not a weight-loss one (see the Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide guide). Discuss the available evidence with the patient — reassuring regarding malformations, more mixed regarding gestational weight gain/gestational diabetes/hypertension (see the same guide) — without creating unwarranted alarm or false reassurance. 5 key messages for counseling: GLP-1/GIP-slowed gastric emptying can reduce absorption of oral contraceptives — discuss it proactively, not reactively. Fertility recovery from weight loss can occur before the patient notices the menstrual change. Preconception washout varies by molecule — there is no single rule for "the GLP-1s." Facing an inadvertent pregnancy, stopping the drug is the immediate step — evidence on malformations is reassuring so far, but evidence on maternal metabolic/hypertensive outcomes is more mixed and warrants active pregnancy follow-up, not just reassurance. The real teratogen in diabetes is uncontrolled hyperglycemia, not the drug itself — do not stop an antidiabetic agent without an already-defined replacement plan.

fichas.texto: The approach to metformin once pregnancy is confirmed depends on why it was prescribed — it is not a single rule: PMOS with ovulation induction/insulin resistance: depending on the clinical context it is continued in early pregnancy or stopped on confirming pregnancy — an individualized, not automatic, decision. Many of these patients reach pregnancy already on metformin and/or myo-inositol as part of their baseline metabolic management (see the PMOS and Myo-inositol guides) — there is no teratogenicity signal for metformin requiring its immediate discontinuation upon confirming pregnancy, unlike GLP-1/GIP analogues (see the Inadvertent pregnancy guide). Prediabetes: individualize according to glycemic control and risk factors. ADA (2026 Standards of Care) does not position metformin as routine in isolated gestational prediabetes — its use follows the same individualization logic as in non-pregnant high-risk patients (elevated BMI, prior GDM, PMOS). NICE (NG3) is somewhat more permissive when risk factors for frank gestational diabetes coexist, where metformin may be anticipated as part of early management if glycemia warrants it — neither guideline indicates it routinely in isolated prediabetes without another risk factor. Pregestational diabetes: ADA prioritizes insulin as first-choice treatment (type 1 and, in most cases, type 2) due to metformin's transplacental passage and a preference for more predictable control; it reserves metformin as an adjunct in type 2 diabetes with high insulin resistance/high requirements, not as monotherapy. NICE (NG3) accepts metformin as first-line or adjunctive therapy in pregestational type 2 diabetes, adding insulin if the glycemic target is not reached — a stance more favorable to oral therapy than ADA's. Gestational diabetes: metformin as a second-line agent versus insulin per ADA (insulin as the preferred first line, metformin as an acceptable alternative after discussing transplacental passage with the patient); NICE (NG3) accepts metformin as a reasonable first line before insulin, barring contraindication or lack of response — see also the algorithm already described in the Gestational Diabetes guide. Summary of the ADA vs. NICE divergence: both agree that uncontrolled hyperglycemia, not metformin, is the real teratogen, but they differ in how much weight they give oral metformin versus insulin: ADA tends to favor insulin as first-line therapy in overt diabetes (pregestational and gestational), reserving metformin as an adjunct or an alternative discussed case by case; NICE accepts metformin more broadly as a reasonable first line in several scenarios. Neither guideline diverges on PMOS, where the decision is individualized for reasons unrelated to fetal safety. Key counseling point: the demonstrated teratogen in this context is uncontrolled hyperglycemia — not metformin itself. This should guide the decision not to abruptly stop an antidiabetic agent without an already-defined replacement plan (insulin or another scheme). Offspring follow-up (MiG TOFU): follow-up of the MiG trial children at 2 years (Diabetes Care 2011) and 7-9 years (BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care 2018) assessed body composition and metabolic outcomes after in-utero metformin exposure — with no signal of harm that would contraindicate its use in gestational diabetes; this is the longest-term support available for this specific indication.

fichas.texto: Metformin: compatible with breastfeeding — infant exposure via milk is generally <0.5% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose, with no adverse effects reported (LactMed, updated 15 August 2026; greater caution in newborns, preterm infants, and infants with renal impairment). LactMed also lists a postpartum restart schedule of 500 mg every 12 hours from day one — useful if an immediate postpartum restart is chosen. Semaglutide: in the only dedicated study to date (Diab et al., Nutrients 2024; 8 women, SC doses 0.25-1 mg/week), semaglutide was not detectable in any of the milk samples analyzed after subcutaneous administration. The authors themselves note the data remain limited — long-term follow-up and data on maternal nutrition/milk composition are lacking. Do not automatically extrapolate this data (subcutaneous semaglutide) to oral formulations. Tirzepatide: per the Zepbound label (DailyMed, section 8.2), in 11 breastfeeding women after a single 5 mg SC dose, tirzepatide was undetectable in 164 of 171 milk samples; the cumulative amount in the remaining 7 samples represented <0.02% of the administered maternal dose — a reassuring figure, though it comes from a single dose, not continuous use over time. With this data it is no longer accurate to say "dedicated studies are lacking" for semaglutide/tirzepatide in lactation — they do exist, although small and short-term. Still distinguish the real risk of infant exposure (low, per this preliminary data) from the mere convenience of restarting maternal treatment as soon as possible — two distinct considerations that should not be blended when counseling the patient.
